summary: The note presents the High Rise Harvests project in downtown Los Angeles as a case study of rooftop rainwater harvesting for urban agriculture. Custom systems capture and filter rainwater for drip irrigation, cutting water use and producing food locally, while workshops and volunteers build community involvement. The project overcame structural and regulatory hurdles and is inspiring similar efforts in other cities, with IoT integration expected next.
one_line: Case study of Los Angeles' High Rise Harvests project, which uses harvested rooftop rainwater to irrigate urban farms efficiently and inspire similar projects.
key_facts: High Rise Harvests is a rooftop gardening project in downtown Los Angeles, initiated in January 2024.
The project is spearheaded by sustainability advocate John Fields and a coalition of urban farmers.
Each garden has a custom rainwater harvesting system that captures and stores rainwater in the wet season for use in the dry months, eliminating the need for municipal water irrigation.
The multi-tiered filtration process, refined over a trial period between September and November 2024, uses pre-filtration, finer filters, and storage in large cisterns equipped with UV filters.
The gardens use drip irrigation and soil moisture sensors that provide real-time data so water is supplied only when necessary.
Farm manager Rebecca Lee reports about 30% less water usage compared to conventional irrigation methods.
The gardens provided over 2,000 kilograms of produce by August 2024.
Crops include leafy greens, herbs, root vegetables and edible flowers, chosen for short harvest cycles, and vertical farming techniques are used.
The project supplies restaurants and farmers' markets, creating a local economy and reducing the carbon footprint of transporting goods.
Workshops, tours, school field trips and volunteer training sessions form the educational and community component of the project.
Concerns about structural integrity and the added weight of stored water were addressed through careful engineering assessments.
Zoning laws and building codes were not written with rooftop farming in mind; activism and proven benefits led to new guidelines facilitating urban agriculture.
Projects in Chicago, New York and London are taking cues from the Los Angeles model.
Ongoing research is looking at integrating smart technologies like the Internet of Things (IoT) for better resource management and crop yield predictions.
